findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce service
findings.body: The newly added `prisma.credential.update(...)` call has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in this file. It will fail type-check and throw a ReferenceError at runtime as soon as a Salesforce client is constructed.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on every client construction, bypassing credential sync
findings.body: This adds an unconditional refresh against login.salesforce.com every time the service is instantiated. It does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so with credential sync enabled the app still hits Salesforce directly with local keys. It also adds a network round trip on every use, and the refreshed `accessToken` is stored in the DB but never used. The `jsforce.Connection` below is still built from the stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `instance_url`.

findings.title: Computed zod schema keys are meaningless and break the minimum token schema
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a literal string like "[object Object]" or "ZodString", not a wildcard key. The schema therefore requires a property literally named that and accepts nothing as the expiry. In sync mode, `safeParse` on a real token response will always fail, and `access_token` is the only meaningful field. The comment-described behaviour (any numeric property is the expiry, other properties allowed) is not implemented. Use `.passthrough()` or `.catchall()` instead.

findings.title: Unconditionally injects a fake refresh_token and returns the wrong shape
findings.body: When `refresh_token` is missing the code sets it to the literal string "refresh_token", even when sync is off. That string is then persisted and later sent to providers as a real refresh token. The function also returns the safeParse result object `{success, data}`, but callers such as Google (`const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)`; `data: { key }`) store that wrapper instead of the token data. The assignment `data.refresh_token = ...` is also a type error on the minimum schema.

findings.title: Google credential is saved as the safeParse wrapper instead of the key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns `{ success, data }`. The code writes that whole object into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, so the stored key becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}`. `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` then fails on the next load and breaks the Google Calendar credential. It should use `.data`. When the sync endpoint returns the response, `res?.data` on a fetch `Response` is also undefined.

findings.title: Sync-mode response is a raw fetch Response, incompatible with callers' expectations
findings.body: In sync mode this returns a fetch `Response`. Several callers expect something else. Google reads `res.data`. Hubspot treats the result as a parsed `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn` and `.accessToken`. Zoho and Bigin read `tokenInfo.data`, which is axios-specific. All of these get undefined or throw. The fetch also has no `Content-Type` or auth header and no `response.ok` check.

findings.title: Bigin passes credentialId as userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` expects `userId`, but `BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken` passes `credentialId` (the third argument is `credentialId`, and the `biginAuth` method never captures `credential.userId`). In sync mode the self-hoster endpoint receives the wrong `calcomUserId` and can return another user's tokens or fail.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==` and may match undefined
findings.body: A plain `!==` comparison leaks timing information about the secret. The header value is also `string | string[] | undefined`. `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is checked first, so the secret is non-empty, but a timing-safe comparison (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`) should be used for a secret that gates credential writes.

findings.title: Unhandled parse/decrypt/JSON errors and no method check
findings.body: `schema.parse` throws on bad bodies, and `symmetricDecrypt` or `JSON.parse` throw on a bad payload or wrong key. All of these surface as unhandled 500s instead of 400s. There is also no HTTP method check, so any method can reach the credential write path. Use `safeParse`, try/catch, and restrict to POST.

findings.title: Credential lookup ignores team credentials and can race to create duplicates
findings.body: The find-then-create flow without a unique constraint can create duplicate credentials when two webhooks arrive concurrently. `findFirst` on `userId` and `appId` also picks an arbitrary credential if the user has several. In addition, `app.slug` is looked up in the DB and then again in `appStoreMetadata`. The `type` is taken from metadata, but there is no check that the app is one that supports sync.

findings.title: Redirect URI hardcoded instead of using appConfig.slug
findings.body: The change replaces `appConfig.slug` with a literal in `add.ts`, but `callback.ts` still builds the redirect URI from `appConfig.slug`. The two can drift out of sync, and the OAuth redirect_uri must match exactly between the authorize and token requests. The change is unrelated to this PR and not needed.

findings.title: Removed error logging and parse failure now throws
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on an invalid response, whereas the old code logged and continued. The previous diagnostic `console.error` with the zod error and MS response was removed, so failures now lose that context. The `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` spread after a throwing parse is dead logic.
